paras: The Marion lynching threat was a lynching scare in Marion, Perry County, Alabama, on Sunday, August 7, 1910, after night watchman Calhoun Watters was shot and Black men were jailed as suspects. Crowds of country citizens gathered and a lynching at one time seemed likely, but no attack on the jail took place. By the end of the month the men were seeking release on bond, with the evidence against them described as all circumstantial.

Watters had been Marion's night watchman for about eighteen months, after living in East Perry and serving as assistant doorkeeper of the state House. According to the Montgomery Advertiser's correspondent, he "had a difficulty with General Moore, a negro," the night before the shooting and had been warned to stay on guard.

At about 4:30 Sunday morning, walking home with Jake Hopper along the sidewalk by the King House, Watters was hit in the neck by a load of bird shot fired by an unknown person from an upstairs window of the hotel. General Moore, his father General Moore Sr., and Tom Sullivan, all described as Black, were arrested at once and kept well guarded in jail.

Through the day citizens from the country came and went, and the Advertiser wrote that "at one time it looked as if a lynching might occur." The Birmingham Age-Herald reported rumors of "the probable lynching of the entre [entire] band," but said no demonstration was made. Both papers credited the opening of the fall circuit court and the arrival of Judge Miller on Sunday evening with calming the crowd.

The grand jury took up the shooting as its first business on August 8, and the sheriff's department claimed it had evidence of a conspiracy by "a band of lawless negroes" to assassinate the officers. The grand jury remanded the men to jail for further investigation, and a habeas corpus hearing before Probate Judge Shivers was set for August 29. That hearing, now for four men, was postponed a week; the Age-Herald expected them to be released on bond because the evidence was circumstantial and Watters had nearly recovered.
A town reward, supplemented by a citizens' reward, reached about $500, and no report of an indictment, trial or the habeas ruling was found.

The coverage found comes from two Alabama dailies, the Montgomery Advertiser and the Birmingham Age-Herald, each through a Marion special correspondent, and no Black-press coverage was found. The Advertiser's headline, "Marion Excited Over Attempt by Assassin," centered the shooting, while the Age-Herald praised citizens for being "willing to allow the law to take its course with negro would-be assassins," treating the accused as guilty. Later notes on the habeas proceedings ran as brief items amid local news, and it was the Age-Herald that reported the evidence was all circumstantial.
The papers differ on how many men were held: the Advertiser named three, the Age-Herald first said two and later four.

accounts.label: Sheriff's department claim (Age-Herald)

framing.detail: The Advertiser headlined 'Marion Excited Over Attempt by Assassin' and reported the lynching danger flatly, crediting the court's opening with calming the crowd.
The Age-Herald's headline praised citizens for being willing to 'allow the law to take its course with negro would-be assassins', presenting the accused as guilty before any hearing.
Late-August notes treated the case as routine court news, reporting the circumstantial evidence and expected bond.

Marion; the shot came from an upstairs window of the King House (hotel).

Accused of attempting to assassinate Night Watchman Watters; the sheriff's department claimed a conspiracy by 'a band of lawless negroes' to assassinate the officers.
Citizens from the country who gathered in Marion; no leaders or numbers named.

A habeas corpus hearing to secure bond was set for Monday, Aug. 29, then postponed a week; the evidence was described as all circumstantial and release on bond was expected. No final outcome was found.
